content: A paramedic is a highly trained medical professional who typically operates as part of an emergency medical service team. Their primary role is to respond to medical and trauma emergencies in pre-hospital settings. Paramedics provide critical emergency treatment and, when necessary, transport patients to facilities capable of delivering definitive care, such as hospitals, for further evaluation or follow-up care. The term paramedic can have different meanings depending on the jurisdiction. In some regions, it refers to any member of an ambulance crew, while in others, such as the United Kingdom, the title is legally protected. In these areas, individuals must complete specific examinations, clinical placements, and hold valid registration with a governing body to be recognized as paramedics. Despite these legal distinctions, popular media often generalizes the term, leading the public to refer to all emergency medical personnel as paramedics, even if they hold lower qualifications, such as emergency medical technicians (EMTs). Paramedics work in a variety of settings, including government-run public hospital systems, municipal emergency medical services (EMS), fire departments, private hospitals, private ambulance companies, emergency departments, inpatient hospital units, medical clinics, doctors' offices, oil rigs, steel mills, air ambulances, and even casinos. The skills performed by paramedics vary significantly by region, but they often include both basic and advanced life support measures. These may involve advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) techniques such as manual defibrillation, synchronized cardioversion, transcutaneous pacing, and electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring and interpretation, including 12-lead ECGs. Paramedics are also trained in pediatric care, such as Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) or Pediatric Education for Prehospital Professionals (PEPP), and trauma care, including Prehospital Trauma Life Support (PHTLS) or Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS). Airway management is a critical skill for paramedics, encompassing procedures like endotracheal and nasotracheal intubation, use of laryngoscopes for airway visualization, removal of foreign bodies with Magill forceps, and advanced techniques such as rapid sequence intubation (RSI), surgical cricothyrotomy, or needle cricothyrotomy with trans-tracheal jet insufflation. They may also employ continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) devices. Paramedics are proficient in establishing vascular access for medication administration and fluid resuscitation through peripheral intravenous (IV) cannulation or intraosseous (IO) cannulation, which involves placing a needle into the marrow space of a large bone. They also utilize tools like pulse oximetry and capnography, perform needle thoracotomy for tension pneumothorax, and conduct glucometry for diabetic patients. Additional skills include venous blood sampling, ventilator and IV pump management, and administering medications via various routes, such as intramuscular, subcutaneous, intravenous, sublingual, endotracheal, rectal, oral, intranasal, intraosseous, and buccal. The medications paramedics administer vary widely based on local protocols, medical director preferences, and legal regulations. These drugs may include calcium channel blockers to manage heart rate, sympathomimetics like dopamine for severe hypotension, and respiratory medications such as albuterol. They may also provide pain relief or antiemetics to reduce nausea and vomiting. For chest pain, medications like nitroglycerin, aspirin, and morphine are commonly used. Paramedics also treat cardiac conditions such as myocardial infarction and various dysrhythmias. Globally, the qualifications and roles of paramedics differ. In the United States, there are four levels of prehospital care defined by the Department of Transportation: First Responder, Emergency Medical Technician-Basic (EMT-B), Emergency Medical Technician-Intermediate (EMT-I), and Emergency Medical Technician-Paramedic (EMT-P). Some systems in the U.S. refer to both EMT-Ps and EMT-Is as paramedics. In Canada, there are three levels of paramedics: Primary Care Paramedic (equivalent to EMT-B), Advanced Care Paramedic (standard paramedic), and Critical Care Paramedic, often employed in flight paramedic roles. In Europe and some Canadian cities, prehospital care may involve doctors, nurses, and medical students working alongside or instead of paramedics. Other regions, like Hong Kong, are transitioning to paramedic-staffed systems. Paramedics may operate under the indirect supervision of a physician, as in the United States, where they follow standing protocols (off-line medical control) or consult directly with physicians via phone or radio (on-line medical control). In contrast, paramedics in the United Kingdom often function as autonomous practitioners, using their clinical judgment to diagnose and prescribe treatments. In popular media, paramedics have been prominently featured in various television shows and films. The 1970s series Emergency. depicted the work of paramedics in the Los Angeles County Fire Department and inspired the development of paramedic programs across the U.S. and encouraged many to pursue careers in emergency medicine. Other portrayals include the Discovery Health Channel's Paramedics, the 1988 comedy Paramedics, and Martin Scorsese's 1999 film Bringing Out the Dead, which follows a burned-out paramedic haunted by his past. Television series like Third Watch and Saved have also explored the lives and challenges of paramedics, highlighting their critical role in emergency medical care.
